prompt.context: Our client is a paper manufacturing company specializing in store label tissue paper. This covers toilet paper, paper towels, napkins, and facial tissues. The client's key customers are grocery chains in the Western US. They would like to double in size, but this is a slow-growing market — it has been growing at 8–9% a year, but has hit a plateau. They have hired us to see how we can re-accelerate growth and if this goal is attainable.
prompt.question: How can the client re-accelerate growth and double in size?

clarifying_info.q: Where are the client's plants located?
clarifying_info.a: The firm has two plants, one near Las Vegas and one in Idaho.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the biggest customers and where are they?
clarifying_info.a: The biggest customers are in the Rockies and in California.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the total market?
clarifying_info.a: The whole market for these products is 500M cases per year (all four kinds combined). 400M cases are branded and 100M are store label.

clarifying_info.q: How is the store label market (100M cases) broken down by channel?
clarifying_info.a: 40M sold in supermarkets, 30M in mass market stores (e.g., Walmart), 20M in club stores (e.g., Sam's Club, Costco), and 10M in dollar stores.

clarifying_info.q: How do customers make purchasing decisions?
clarifying_info.a: Customers (mostly chains) make their purchasing decisions regionally, not store by store.

clarifying_info.q: What is the revenue per case?
clarifying_info.a: Retailers pay $20 per case of product.

clarifying_info.q: What does it cost to ship to California?
clarifying_info.a: It costs $1 to ship a case from either plant to California.

clarifying_info.q: What does it cost to ship to the East Coast (e.g., Boston)?
clarifying_info.a: It costs $750 to send a truckload to Boston plus $0.75 per mile; the width of the US is 3,000 miles. A truck holds 1,000 cases.

exhibits.title: Case Overview Page
exhibits.shows: The first page of the case containing the case prompt, Phase 1 market data bullets, and Phase 2 cost data bullets as presented in the casebook.
exhibits.data: Total market: 500M cases; branded 400M, store label 100M; channel split: supermarkets 40M, mass market 30M, club 20M, dollar stores 10M; price $20/case; shipping to CA $1/case; truckload to Boston $750 + $0.75/mile; truck capacity 1,000 cases; US width 3,000 miles

framework: Define the goal: double in size in a slow-growth (8–9%, now plateaued) store-label tissue market
Assess current geographic footprint: two Western US plants serving Western customers only
Evaluate market size and share: 100M store-label cases; identify addressable segments (supermarkets, mass, club, dollar)
Analyze expansion options: (a) ship from existing plants to East Coast, (b) open new plants in the East
Calculate shipping economics to determine feasibility of option (a)
Evaluate product mix: which of the four tissue categories (toilet paper, napkins, paper towels, facial tissues) sell best under store label
Synthesize: recommend geographic and product-mix strategy to reach doubling goal

questions.prompt: Phase 2 – Shipping cost analysis: How much does it cost to ship a truckload to Boston vs. California, and what revenue remains after shipping in each case?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify all cost variables (fixed truckload fee, per-mile rate, distance, truck capacity), calculate total shipping cost per truckload, then per case, and compare gross revenue remaining after shipping costs for both geographies.

math.setup: Truckload to Boston: $750 fixed + $0.75/mile × 3,000 miles = total truckload shipping cost. Revenue per truckload = 1,000 cases × $20/case. Compare net after shipping for Boston vs. California.
steps: $2,250 + $750 fixed = $3,000 total shipping cost per truckload to Boston
Revenue after Boston shipping = $20,000 − $3,000 = $17,000 per truckload
Revenue after California shipping = $20,000 − $1,000 = $19,000 per truckload
math.answer: Shipping to Boston costs $3,000 per truckload (vs. $1,000 to California), leaving $17,000 vs. $19,000 after shipping — a $2,000 difference per truckload, or $2 per case. Shipping to the East Coast from current plants is significantly more expensive and erodes margins.

questions.prompt: Phase 3 – Product mix: Is the store-label split even across the four tissue categories? Which categories likely have stronger store-label share?
questions.guidance: Candidate should reason that branded strength varies by category. Facial tissues (Kleenex is a generic synonym) and paper towels have strong brand identities, so consumers are more loyal to brands in those categories. Napkins and toilet paper have weaker brand differentiation, making store-label more competitive there.

brainstorming.prompt: Given the geographic and product-mix insights, what strategies could the client pursue to double in size?

categories.name: Geographic Expansion
ideas: Open new plants on the East Coast to serve Eastern grocery chains at competitive shipping costs
Target the same national chains already served in the West (same chains operate in the East)
Consider locations in less expensive areas to keep plant costs low

categories.name: Product Mix Optimization
ideas: Increase production of napkins and toilet paper, where store-label demand is highest
Reduce or deprioritize facial tissues and paper towels where branded loyalty is stronger
Tailor product mix by region based on local retailer preferences

categories.name: Channel Expansion
ideas: Currently focused on supermarkets; explore mass market (30M cases) and club stores (20M cases)
Dollar store channel (10M cases) may be addressable with lower-cost SKUs

categories.name: Customer Relationships
ideas: Deepen relationships with existing Western grocery chains to capture more wallet share
Leverage regional purchasing decisions to sign multi-region contracts with national chains

recommendation: The client cannot double in size by shipping from existing Western plants to the East Coast — shipping costs are prohibitive ($3,000/truckload vs. $1,000 to California).
The primary growth lever is opening new plants in the Eastern US to serve the large untapped Eastern store-label market (same national chains operate there).
Secondary lever: optimize the product mix by shifting capacity toward napkins and toilet paper, where store-label competition with brands is strongest.
risks: Capital investment and execution risk of building/acquiring new Eastern plants
Slower time-to-market if plant construction takes several years
Eastern market may have existing store-label competitors not present in the West
next_steps: Conduct site selection and cost analysis for Eastern plant locations
Model full P&L for an Eastern plant scenario to confirm doubling is financially viable
Negotiate with Eastern grocery chain buyers to gauge demand before committing capital
Review production capacity utilization and shift mix toward napkins and toilet paper in existing plants
